pedagogy.summary: These word problems apply multiplication of a fraction by a whole number in context — 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza, four 2/3-metre ribbon pieces. The core idea is a/b × n as n copies of a/b (repeated addition of a unit-fraction multiple), and the practical twist is interpreting an improper-fraction product back in context: 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, but you must BUY 2 whole pizzas. Teach it as repeated groups on a bar or number line, estimate between whole numbers (6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5), convert the improper result to a mixed number, and round or interpret according to the situation.
bestPractices: Model as repeated equal groups — n copies of a/b — accumulating on a bar or number line so the product is built, not just computed
Multiply only the numerator by the whole number (n × a/b = na/b); keep the denominator as the unchanged unit
Estimate between which whole numbers the product lies before computing (6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5)
Convert the improper product to a mixed number and INTERPRET it in context (round pizzas needed up to a whole)
Distinguish 'how much is eaten' (exact mixed number) from 'how many must be bought' (rounded up)
keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated fraction jumps of a/b
Repeated-groups bar (n copies of the fraction) accumulating past wholes
Improper → mixed conversion of the product
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too (4 × 2/3 → 8/12), scaling the unit as well as the count
Adds the whole number to the fraction instead of multiplying (3/8 + 5)
Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up
Chooses the wrong operation because the repeated-groups structure is not read

learn.summary: Learners solve word problems that multiply a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) by treating the product as n copies of the unit-fraction multiple, accumulating them on a bar or number line, converting the improper result to a mixed number, and interpreting that result in context — distinguishing exactly how much is used (e.g. 1 7/8 pizzas eaten) from how many whole units must be bought (2 pizzas). Core examples: 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza; four ribbon pieces of 2/3 metre; estimating that 6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5.

activities.title: Build the product by stacking repeated fraction groups
feedback: If the denominator changed (e.g. 4 × 2/3 written as 8/12), return to the groups: 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — only the number of thirds grows, each piece is still a third.
If the whole number was added instead (3/8 + 5), redraw the five groups of 3/8 and name it aloud as 'five lots of 3/8' before writing ×.
If the answer was left improper, prompt: how many whole bars and how much extra does 15/8 make?
activities.rationale: Modelling multiplication as accumulating repeated groups on a visual model builds na/b concretely and confronts the documented error of scaling the denominator; keeping the denominator fixed shows the unit is unchanged.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Take a catering problem: 5 friends, each eats 3/8 of a pizza — work out the total eaten by building copies, not by jumping to a rule.
Stack five copies of a 3/8 bar (or draw five jumps of 3/8 on a number line) and track the running total: 3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8, 15/8, noting when the total crosses a whole.
Record the result as the improper fraction 15/8 and convert it to the mixed number 1 7/8.
State in words: the top number (count of eighths) grows while the denominator stays eighths — the unit does not change.
Repeat the build for 4 × 2/3 (thirds accumulating to 8/3 = 2 2/3) to generalise.
If a live builder is available, set the fraction and the count and watch copies stack with a running total snapping the whole-number boundaries; otherwise draw each jump by hand.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeatedly adding that fraction: n copies of a/b accumulate to na/b, so only the numerator (count of unit fractions) grows while the denominator stays the fixed unit.

activities.title: Interpret the result: eaten versus bought
feedback: If 15/8 or 1 7/8 is given as the number to buy, ask: 'You can't buy 7/8 of a pizza — how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' The multiplication is correct; only the interpretation is missing.
If rounding is applied where it isn't needed (ribbon length), point out that 2 2/3 metres is a valid measurement — rounding depends on whether the unit can be partial.
Reinforce estimating first: if 6 × 3/4 was expected to be a whole number, note that 18/4 = 4 1/2 lies between 4 and 5, as the estimate predicts, so the product is not a whole number.
activities.rationale: Interpreting the improper product in context — distinguishing the exact amount from the whole quantity a situation demands — is the real purpose of the word problem; estimating between whole numbers provides a reasonableness check.
sourceClaims: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Using the computed total 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, decide how many whole pizzas must be ordered, given you cannot buy part of a pizza.
Explain why 1 7/8 rounds UP to 2 here, and why the question 'how much is eaten' keeps the exact 1 7/8.
Answer a contrast pair: 'How much pizza is eaten?' (1 7/8, exact) and 'How many whole pizzas must be bought?' (2, rounded up).
For the ribbon problem, state 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres and decide whether rounding is needed (it is not — a length can be a mixed number).
Before computing another problem, estimate between which two whole numbers the product lies, e.g. 6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper-fraction product must be read back into the situation: the exact mixed number answers 'how much', but 'how many whole units are needed' may require rounding up — and some quantities (like length) sensibly stay as mixed numbers.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with targeted questions
feedback: A product with a changed denominator (8/12), often then 'simplified' to 2/3, reveals the denominator-scaling error — reteach via repeated groups.
A correct computation but a fractional buy-quantity shows a missing interpretation step, not a broken method.
An answer near 5 3/8 or an addition of whole and fraction signals the wrong operation was chosen — redraw the groups and name them before writing ×.
activities.rationale: A short set of discriminating items separates computational slips, the denominator misconception, and interpretation gaps, and checks transfer to a new context. Recognition items check reasoning but do not by themselves show independent construction, so pair them with an end-to-end solve.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
learnerActions: Answer: 4 × 2/3 = ? Choose and justify from 8/12, 8/3, 2 2/3, explaining why 8/12 is wrong (denominator scaled) and showing that 8/3 and 2 2/3 are the same value.
Fill in the blank: n × a/b = __/b, stating the rule in your own words.
Estimate on a scale 'between which two whole numbers is 6 × 3/4?' and place it.
Solve a fresh word problem (e.g. a new fraction × whole context) end to end: build, compute na/b, convert, and interpret whether to round.
Explain in a sentence what a party host should order for a group, separating 'eaten' from 'bought'.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners compute na/b (numerator only), convert to a mixed number, interpret in context, estimate between whole numbers, and transfer the method to a new word problem.

constraints: Enforce or emphasise numerator-only scaling: when multiplying, the denominator (unit) stays fixed; a builder that makes multiplying the denominator impossible is a scaffold, but learners must also be able to state and apply the rule without the tool.

Recognition/multiple-choice items (e.g. choosing 8/3 over 8/12) check whether the learner can judge answers but do not on their own demonstrate independent construction; include at least one full build-and-interpret task.
A tap-to-reveal static worked pair illustrates the accumulation and interpretation but cannot let the learner vary the count — use it as an example, not as the main practice where varying n matters.
Rounding up applies to quantities that must be whole (pizzas to buy); it is not universal — lengths and similar measures can remain mixed numbers. Always tie rounding to the situation.
A conversational/role-play framing (party-planning host) can pose the 'eaten vs bought' question well, but the accumulation itself benefits from a visual surface (bar or number line).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic audit (independently re-checked): 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8; 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3; 6 × 3/4 = 18/4 = 4 1/2, which lies between 4 and 5. The original candidate draft had written '18/4 = 4 2/3' in the interpret activity's estimation feedback; this is incorrect and now reads 4 1/2 at every occurrence.

The source row rated a 3D/physical representation as a 'poor fit' with the claim that '3D adds nothing' for planar repeated groups; this categorical modality claim is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped. A 3D or physical representation is simply a different, non-required experience, not evidence that one medium is superior.

CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; no new verification was performed. The IES/WWC source is marked verified:true in the row — this reflects legacy metadata, not a re-check during this rewrite.

probeDeeper: In (a), 15/8 pizzas are eaten — can you buy 15/8 of a pizza? How many whole ones do you need?
Between which two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie, without computing exactly?
Show 4 × 2/3 as jumps on a number line — how many thirds altogether?
Estimate (b) — more or less than 2 metres? more or less than 3?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten; you must buy 2 whole pizzas. (b) 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the denominator as well: 4 × 2/3 → 8/12 (scales the unit along with the count)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to repeated groups — four lots of 2/3 is 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — on a number line so only the count of thirds grows; the third stays the unit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product has a changed denominator (8/12 rather than 8/3); often then 'simplified' to 2/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up: reports 15/8 or 1 7/8 as the number to buy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'you can't buy part of a pizza; how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' — the multiplication is sound, only the interpretation is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computation correct but the buy-quantity is given as a fraction/mixed number rather than 2 whole pizzas

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds instead of multiplies, or chooses the wrong operation: 3/8 + 5, because the repeated-groups structure is not read
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the groups first — 5 people each with 3/8 — and name it as 5 lots of 3/8 before writing ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An addition of the whole and the fraction, or an answer near 5 3/8; no repeated-groups working

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies the denominator, or adds instead of multiplies; no repeated-groups model.
responseLevels.full: Multiplies correctly (numerator only), converts to a mixed number, interprets in context (rounds pizzas needed up to 2), estimates between whole numbers, and transfers to a new fraction × whole word problem.
responseLevels.partial: Computes na/b correctly (15/8, 8/3) but cannot convert/interpret the improper result in context — leaves it improper or fails to round the buy-quantity up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, showing your working: (a) Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how much pizza is eaten in total, and how many whole pizzas must be bought? (b) A ribbon is cut into pieces each 2/3 of a metre long — how long are 4 pieces altogether?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method catches the two faults a bare answer hides: whether the denominator was wrongly scaled (4 × 2/3 → 8/12 instead of 8/3) and whether the improper product was interpreted in context. Part (a) is engineered to separate 'how much is eaten' (1 7/8, exact) from 'how many to buy' (2, rounded up) — a child who reports 1 7/8 pizzas to buy has computed correctly but not interpreted. A child who multiplies the denominator, or adds instead, reveals a broken model of a/b × n.
